statement: Every small [abelian category](c:abelian-category) $\mathcal{A}$ has a full, faithful and [exact functor](c:exact-functor) into the [category of modules](c:module-category) over some ring $R$.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal{A}$ is an [abelian category](c:abelian-category).
$\mathcal{A}$ is a [small category](c:small-category): its objects form a set.

conclusion: There are a ring $R$ and an exact, full and faithful functor from $\mathcal{A}$ to the category of $R$-modules.

proofs.name: Left exact functors
proofs.slogan: Embed the small abelian category into the Grothendieck category of left exact functors, then read modules over the endomorphism ring of an injective cogenerator.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline of the published proof. The size hypothesis makes the category of functors on $\mathcal{A}$ a category with sets of morphisms.

roles.why: The abelian structure makes each representable functor left exact and makes the embedding exact.
Smallness gives a set of representables, so the functor category has a generator and an injective cogenerator.

steps.slogan: Send each object to the left exact functor it represents.
steps.detail: For $a \in \mathcal{A}$ put $H^a = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{A}}(a,-)$, a left exact additive functor $\mathcal{A} \to \mathrm{Ab}$. The [Yoneda embedding](c:yoneda-embedding) $a \mapsto H^a$ is a fully faithful functor from $\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{op}}$ into the category $\mathcal{L}$ of left exact additive functors.

steps.slogan: Show that left exact functors form a [Grothendieck category](c:grothendieck-category).
steps.detail: Kernels and products in $\mathcal{L}$ are computed pointwise, and $\mathcal{L}$ is abelian with exact filtered colimits. The product of all the $H^a$ is a generator of $\mathcal{L}$.

steps.slogan: Choose an injective [cogenerator](c:cogenerator) $E$ of $\mathcal{L}$ and set $R = \mathrm{End}(E)$.
steps.detail: A Grothendieck category has enough injectives and a generator, so it has an injective cogenerator $E$. The functor $T = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{L}}(-,E)$ lands in $R$-modules. It is exact because $E$ is injective, and faithful because $E$ is a cogenerator.

steps.slogan: Identify $T(H^a)$ with the value $E(a)$ and show that $E$ is an exact functor on $\mathcal{A}$.
steps.detail: By the Yoneda lemma $T(H^a) = \mathrm{Hom}(H^a,E) = E(a)$, with $R$ acting by natural transformations. The functor $E$ is left exact because it lies in $\mathcal{L}$. It is right exact because $E$ is injective and an epimorphism $a \to a''$ gives a monomorphism $H^{a''} \to H^a$.

steps.slogan: Check that the exact functor $a \mapsto E(a)$ is full as well as faithful.
steps.detail: Faithfulness follows because $E$ is a cogenerator. For fullness, the cited proofs use that each $H^a$ is a finitely presented object of $\mathcal{L}$, so that $R$-linear maps $E(a) \to E(b)$ come from morphisms of $\mathcal{L}$, and these come from $\mathcal{A}$ by step 1.

concepts.c:abelian-category: The theorem embeds an abelian category, and its exactness is what the embedding keeps.
concepts.c:exact-functor: The embedding must preserve exact sequences, so diagram chases transfer to modules.
concepts.c:module-category: The target of the embedding is a category of modules over a ring.
concepts.c:small-category: Smallness makes the functor category on $\mathcal{A}$ well behaved, with sets of morphisms.
concepts.c:yoneda-embedding: Representable functors give the first full embedding of the category.
concepts.c:grothendieck-category: This property gives an injective cogenerator and an exact functor to modules.
concepts.c:cogenerator: The injective cogenerator defines the ring $R$ and makes the functor faithful.

source.ref: B. Mitchell, The full imbedding theorem, American Journal of Mathematics 86 (1964), 619-637; P. Freyd, Abelian Categories, Harper and Row, New York, 1964; C. A. Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra, Cambridge University Press, 1994, Theorem 1.6.1
source.note: The steps follow the left exact functor proof of Freyd and Mitchell as presented by Weibel; the fullness step is only summarised here.

statement: Let $X$ be a closed smooth [spin](c:spin-manifold) 4-manifold whose [intersection form](c:intersection-form) is indefinite. Then $b_2(X) \ge \tfrac{10}{8}\,|\sigma(X)| + 2$, where $\sigma$ is the signature.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a closed, oriented, smooth 4-manifold with a [spin structure](c:spin-manifold).
The [intersection form](c:intersection-form) of $X$ on $H^2(X;\mathbb{R})$ is indefinite.

proofs.name: Pin(2)-equivariant Seiberg-Witten map
proofs.slogan: Approximate the Pin(2)-equivariant Seiberg-Witten map of the spin structure and bound the dimensions by an equivariant Borsuk-Ulam theorem.
proofs.scope: The outline takes $b_1(X) = 0$; spin surgery on circles removes $b_1$ and keeps $b_2$ and $\sigma$. The case $\sigma > 0$ follows by reversing the orientation, and $\sigma = 0$ follows from indefiniteness, which gives $b_2 \ge 2$.

roles.why: The spin structure makes the spinor bundles quaternionic, which gives the Pin(2) symmetry and the index $m$.
Indefiniteness gives $b^\pm \ge 1$, which settles $\sigma = 0$ and excludes definite forms.

steps.slogan: Write the [Seiberg-Witten equations](c:seiberg-witten-equations) of the spin structure and note their Pin(2) symmetry.
steps.detail: A spin structure makes the spinor bundles quaternionic. The Seiberg-Witten equations are then invariant under $\mathrm{Pin}(2) = S^1 \cup jS^1 \subset Sp(1)$, which acts on spinors by quaternion multiplication and on 1-forms by the sign character.

steps.slogan: Compute the quaternionic index $m$ of the spin Dirac operator from the signature.
steps.detail: The Atiyah-Singer index theorem and the Hirzebruch signature theorem give complex index $-\sigma(X)/8$ for the Dirac operator. Its kernel and cokernel are quaternionic, so the quaternionic index is $m = -\sigma(X)/16$.

steps.slogan: Approximate the Seiberg-Witten map by a Pin(2)-equivariant map of representation spheres.
steps.detail: Finite dimensional approximation gives a Pin(2)-equivariant map $f\colon (\mathbb{H}^{a} \oplus \tilde{\mathbb{R}}^{c})^+ \to (\mathbb{H}^{a-m} \oplus \tilde{\mathbb{R}}^{c+b^+})^+$, where $\tilde{\mathbb{R}}$ is the sign representation. On the $S^1$-fixed points it is the linear inclusion induced by $d^+$.

steps.slogan: Prove a Pin(2) Borsuk-Ulam inequality with [equivariant K-theory](c:equivariant-k-theory).
steps.detail: Furuta shows, by comparing the Pin(2)-equivariant K-theory of the two representation spheres, that such a map $f$ with $m > 0$ forces $b^+ \ge 2m + 1$.

steps.slogan: Convert the inequality $b^+ \ge 2m+1$ into the bound on $b_2$.
steps.detail: For $\sigma < 0$ we have $2m = |\sigma|/8$, so $b^+ \ge |\sigma|/8 + 1$. Then $b_2 = 2b^+ + |\sigma| \ge \tfrac{10}{8}|\sigma| + 2$. For $\sigma > 0$ reverse the orientation, and for $\sigma = 0$ use $b^+, b^- \ge 1$.

concepts.c:spin-manifold: A spin structure gives the quaternionic spinors and the Pin(2) symmetry.
concepts.c:intersection-form: Its indefiniteness settles the case of zero signature and excludes definite forms.
concepts.c:seiberg-witten-equations: Their symmetry and solutions give the map that the proof approximates.
concepts.c:equivariant-k-theory: It detects the dimension inequality for Pin(2)-equivariant maps of spheres.

source.ref: M. Furuta, Monopole equation and the 11/8-conjecture, Mathematical Research Letters 8 (2001), 279-291
source.note: The steps outline Furuta's proof: Seiberg-Witten map, finite dimensional approximation, and the Pin(2)-equivariant K-theory argument.

statement: For natural numbers $m \ne n$, the [Fermat numbers](c:fermat-number) $F_m = 2^{2^m}+1$ and $F_n = 2^{2^n}+1$ are [coprime](c:coprime-integers).

hypotheses.text: The natural numbers $m$ and $n$ are different.

conclusion: The [greatest common divisor](c:greatest-common-divisor) of $F_m$ and $F_n$ is $1$.

proofs.name: Product formula
proofs.slogan: Write $F_n - 2$ as the product of the earlier Fermat numbers, so a common divisor of $F_m$ and $F_n$ divides $2$.
proofs.scope: All pairs $m \ne n$; by symmetry we take $m < n$.

roles.why: It lets us order the indices, so $F_m$ is one of the factors of the product.

steps.slogan: Order the indices so that $m < n$ and name the common divisor $d$.
steps.detail: The greatest common divisor is symmetric in its two arguments, and $m \ne n$. So we may assume $m < n$ and put $d = \gcd(F_m, F_n)$.

steps.slogan: Prove that $F_n - 2 = \prod_{k<n} F_k$ by induction on $n$.
steps.detail: For $n=0$ both sides equal $1$. If it holds for $n$, then $\prod_{k<n+1} F_k = (F_n-2)F_n = (2^{2^n}-1)(2^{2^n}+1) = 2^{2^{n+1}}-1 = F_{n+1}-2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $d$ divides both $F_n$ and $F_n - 2$, hence divides $2$.
steps.detail: Since $m < n$, the number $F_m$ is a factor of the product, so $d \mid F_m \mid F_n - 2$. Also $d \mid F_n$. So $d$ divides the difference $F_n - (F_n - 2) = 2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $F_n$ is odd, so $d$ is not $2$.
steps.detail: The number $2^{2^n}$ is even, so $F_n$ is odd. Since $d \mid F_n$ and $d \mid 2$, we get $d \in \{1, 2\}$ and $d \ne 2$. Hence $d = 1$.

concepts.c:fermat-number: The proof studies the numbers $2^{2^k}+1$ through their product formula.
concepts.c:coprime-integers: The theorem says that two different Fermat numbers are coprime.
concepts.c:greatest-common-divisor: A common divisor $d$ is shown to divide $2$ and then to equal $1$.

source.note: mathlib reduces to $m<n$ with wlog, uses fermatNumber_eq_prod_add_two with gcd_dvd_left and dvd_prod_of_mem to get $d \mid 2$, and odd_fermatNumber to exclude $d=2$.

statement: Let a compact connected Lie group $G$ act on a compact [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) $M$ with a prequantum line bundle, by a [Hamiltonian action](c:hamiltonian-action) with [moment map](c:moment-map) $\mu$. Suppose $0$ is a regular value and $G$ acts freely on $\mu^{-1}(0)$. Then $\dim Q(M)^G = \dim Q(M/\!/G)$, where $Q$ is [geometric quantization](c:geometric-quantization) and $M/\!/G$ is the [symplectic reduction](c:symplectic-reduction).

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a compact symplectic manifold whose symplectic form has a prequantum [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $L$.
A compact connected Lie group $G$ acts on $M$ by a [Hamiltonian action](c:hamiltonian-action) with [moment map](c:moment-map) $\mu$, and the action lifts to $L$.
The value $0$ is regular for $\mu$, and $G$ acts freely on $\mu^{-1}(0)$.

conclusion: The $G$-invariant part of $Q(M)$ and the quantization $Q(M/\!/G)$ of the reduced space have the same dimension.

proofs.name: Analytic localization of the Dirac operator
proofs.slogan: Deform the Spin^c Dirac operator by the moment map and localize its invariant spectrum near $\mu^{-1}(0)$, where it becomes the Dirac operator of the reduced space.
proofs.scope: The case of a free action on $\mu^{-1}(0)$. The family also covers locally free actions and singular reductions, which this outline does not treat.

roles.why: Compactness gives a discrete spectrum and finite dimensional kernels for the Dirac operator.
The action and the moment map define the invariant operator and its deformation by the Kirwan vector field.
Freeness makes $\mu^{-1}(0) \to M/\!/G$ a principal bundle and the reduced space a manifold.

steps.slogan: Define the [geometric quantization](c:geometric-quantization) $Q(M)$ as the index of the Dirac operator twisted by $L$.
steps.detail: Choose a $G$-invariant compatible almost complex structure. The [Spin^c Dirac operator](c:spinc-dirac-operator) $D_L$ on $\Lambda^{0,\bullet}T^*M \otimes L$ is $G$-equivariant, and $Q(M) = \ker D_L^+ - \ker D_L^-$ is a virtual representation of $G$. Its invariant part $Q(M)^G$ is the object to compute.

steps.slogan: Deform the Dirac operator by Clifford multiplication with the Kirwan vector field of $\mu$.
steps.detail: Add $T$ times Clifford multiplication by the vector field generated by $|\mu|^2$ to $D_L$, a deformation of Witten type. On $G$-invariant sections the index does not depend on $T$.

steps.slogan: Show that the low spectrum of the invariant deformed operator concentrates near $\mu^{-1}(0)$ as $T \to \infty$.
steps.detail: The cited paper proves, with Witten-Bismut-Lebeau type estimates, that for large $T$ the small spectrum of the invariant deformed operator lives in a neighborhood of $\mu^{-1}(0)$. Away from it the operator is bounded below by a multiple of $T$.

steps.slogan: Identify the localized operator with a Dirac operator on the [reduced space](c:symplectic-reduction).
steps.detail: Because $G$ acts freely, $\mu^{-1}(0)$ is a [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) over $M/\!/G$, and invariant sections of $L$ near it are sections of the induced bundle on $M/\!/G$. In the normal directions the deformed operator is a harmonic oscillator with a one dimensional ground state. So the localized operator is the Spin^c Dirac operator of $M/\!/G$ up to small error.

steps.slogan: Equate the invariant index of $M$ with the index on the reduced space.
steps.detail: For large $T$ the invariant index of the deformed operator equals the index of the reduced Dirac operator, and the invariant index does not depend on $T$. Hence $\dim Q(M)^G = \dim Q(M/\!/G)$ as virtual dimensions.

concepts.c:symplectic-manifold: The manifold $M$ carries the symplectic form that is quantized.
concepts.c:hamiltonian-action: The action with a moment map defines the reduction and the deformation.
concepts.c:moment-map: Its zero set gives the reduced space and the localization region.
concepts.c:geometric-quantization: Quantization is the index that the proof compares on $M$ and on $M/\!/G$.
concepts.c:symplectic-reduction: The reduced space is where the localized Dirac operator lives.
concepts.c:line-bundle: The prequantum line bundle twists the Dirac operator.
concepts.c:spinc-dirac-operator: Its index defines quantization, and its deformation is localized.
concepts.c:principal-bundle: The zero level set of the moment map is a principal bundle over the reduced space.

source.ref: Y. Tian and W. Zhang, An analytic proof of the geometric quantization conjecture of Guillemin-Sternberg, Inventiones Mathematicae 132 (1998), 229-259
source.note: The steps outline the analytic proof of Tian and Zhang; Meinrenken and Vergne gave other proofs.

statement: The positive [square root](c:square-root) of $2$ is not a [rational number](c:rational-number).

proofs.name: Rational root of a monic polynomial
proofs.slogan: A rational square root of $2$ would be an integer by the rational root theorem, and no integer has square $2$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; there are no hypotheses and no cases.

steps.slogan: Suppose that $\sqrt{2} = q$ for a rational number $q$.
steps.detail: Then $q^2 = 2$, so $q$ is a rational root of the monic integer polynomial $x^2 - 2$. We show that this is impossible.

steps.slogan: Show that a rational root of $x^2 - 2$ is an integer.
steps.detail: Write $q = a/b$ in lowest terms with $b \ge 1$. Then $a^2 = 2b^2$, so $b$ divides $a^2$. Since $a$ and $b$ are coprime, $b = 1$. This is the rational root theorem for a monic polynomial.

steps.slogan: Show that no integer has square $2$, using [prime factorization](c:prime-factorization).
steps.detail: If $a^2 = 2$ with $a$ an integer, the prime $2$ occurs once in the factorization of $2$ but an even number of times in that of $a^2$. Unique factorization forbids this.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give an integer $q$ with $q^2 = 2$, which is impossible. So no rational number has square $2$.

concepts.c:square-root: The number $\sqrt{2}$ is the positive solution of $x^2 = 2$.
concepts.c:rational-number: The proof assumes a fraction $a/b$ and reaches a contradiction.
concepts.c:irrational-number: The theorem says that $\sqrt{2}$ is not a quotient of integers.
concepts.c:prime-factorization: The parity of the exponent of $2$ rules out an integer square.

source.note: mathlib uses Nat.Prime.irrational_sqrt, which combines irrational_sqrt_natCast_iff (a natural number with a rational square root is a perfect square) with Nat.Prime.not_isSquare.

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective variety with [canonical bundle](c:canonical-bundle) $K_X$, and let $L$ be a [big and nef](c:big-and-nef-divisor) line bundle on $X$. Then $H^i(X, K_X \otimes L) = 0$ for every $i > 0$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a smooth complex projective [variety](c:algebraic-variety).
The line bundle $L$ on $X$ is [big and nef](c:big-and-nef-divisor).

conclusion: The [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) groups $H^i(X, K_X \otimes L)$ vanish for all $i > 0$.

proofs.name: Kodaira lemma and covering trick
proofs.slogan: Write the bundle as the round-up of an ample Q-divisor with normal crossing fractional part, take a cyclic cover, and reduce to Kodaira vanishing on the cover.
proofs.scope: The statement for an integral line bundle. The family includes the version for $\mathbb{Q}$-divisors and for [log pairs](c:log-pair), which the same covering argument proves.

roles.why: Smoothness and projectivity allow a log resolution, a smooth finite cover and Kodaira vanishing.
Nef and big gives an ample $\mathbb{Q}$-divisor after a small perturbation.

steps.slogan: Write a multiple of $L$ as an [ample](c:ample-sheaf) divisor plus an effective divisor.
steps.detail: Kodaira's lemma for the big bundle $L$ gives $mL \sim A + E$ with $A$ ample and $E$ effective. For small rational $\varepsilon > 0$ the $\mathbb{Q}$-divisor $L - \varepsilon E = (1-\varepsilon m)L + \varepsilon A$ is nef plus ample, hence ample.

steps.slogan: Blow up $X$ to make the pull-back of $E$ a normal crossing divisor.
steps.detail: Let $\pi\colon X' \to X$ be a log resolution of $E$ with exceptional divisor $F$, so that $\pi^*E + F$ has simple normal crossing support. The bundle $\pi^*L$ is still nef and big.

steps.slogan: Perturb $\pi^*L$ into an ample $\mathbb{Q}$-divisor $D$ with round-up $\pi^*L$.
steps.detail: Put $D = \pi^*(L - \varepsilon E) - \delta F$ for small rational $\delta > 0$ and a suitable choice of $F$. Then $D$ is ample on $X'$, its fractional part is supported on $\pi^*E + F$, and $\lceil D \rceil = \pi^*L$.

steps.slogan: Take a finite cover that makes $f^*D$ integral and contains $K_{X'} + \lceil D \rceil$ as a summand.
steps.detail: Kawamata's [branched cyclic cover](c:branched-cover) $f\colon Y \to X'$ is branched along the components of $\pi^*E + F$ and along general ample divisors. The variety $Y$ is smooth and projective, $f^*D$ is an integral ample divisor, and $H^i(X', K_{X'} \otimes \lceil D \rceil)$ is a direct summand of $H^i(Y, K_Y \otimes f^*D)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $H^i(Y, K_Y \otimes f^*D)$ vanishes by Kodaira vanishing.
steps.detail: Kodaira vanishing on the smooth projective variety $Y$ gives $H^i(Y, K_Y \otimes f^*D) = 0$ for $i > 0$. A direct summand of zero is zero, so $H^i(X', K_{X'} \otimes \pi^*L) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Descend the vanishing from $X'$ to $X$ with the direct image of $K_{X'}$.
steps.detail: Grauert-Riemenschneider vanishing gives $R^j\pi_*K_{X'} = 0$ for $j > 0$, and $\pi_*K_{X'} = K_X$. The projection formula and the Leray spectral sequence give $H^i(X, K_X \otimes L) = H^i(X', K_{X'} \otimes \pi^*L) = 0$.

concepts.c:canonical-bundle: The vanishing concerns line bundles of the form $K_X \otimes L$.
concepts.c:big-and-nef-divisor: This positivity of $L$ is the hypothesis that the proof reduces to ampleness.
concepts.c:algebraic-variety: A smooth projective variety allows resolution, finite covers and Kodaira vanishing.
concepts.c:sheaf-cohomology: The theorem states vanishing of higher cohomology groups of a line bundle.
concepts.c:log-pair: Log pairs carry the more general divisor version that the covering trick proves.
concepts.c:ample-sheaf: Ampleness of the perturbed divisor is what Kodaira vanishing needs.
concepts.c:branched-cover: The cover makes the fractional parts integral and keeps $K_{X'} + \lceil D \rceil$ as a summand.

source.ref: Y. Kawamata, A generalization of Kodaira-Ramanujam's vanishing theorem, Mathematische Annalen 261 (1982), 43-46; E. Viehweg, Vanishing theorems, Journal fuer die reine und angewandte Mathematik 335 (1982), 1-8
source.note: The steps follow the covering-trick argument of the two papers as presented in Lazarsfeld, Positivity in Algebraic Geometry I (2004).

statement: Let $R$ be a reduced irreducible [root system](c:is-root-system) of rank $n$ whose [Weyl group](c:weyl-group) has degrees $d_1, \dots, d_n$, and let $k$ be a positive integer. Then the [constant term](c:constant-term) of $\prod_{\alpha \in R}(1 - e^{\alpha})^k$ in the group algebra of the weight lattice is $\prod_{i=1}^n \binom{k d_i}{k}$.

hypotheses.text: $R$ is a reduced irreducible [root system](c:is-root-system) of rank $n$, and $d_1, \dots, d_n$ are the degrees of its Weyl group.
The exponent $k$ is a positive integer.

proofs.name: Double affine Hecke algebras
proofs.slogan: Realize the Macdonald weight through a double affine Hecke algebra, compute the norm of $1$ with intertwiners and duality, and let $q \to 1$.
proofs.scope: The classical identity, obtained from the $q$-version that Cherednik proves for all reduced root systems. The family includes the $q$-analogues, the unequal-parameter versions, and the Dyson conjecture as the case $A_{n-1}$.

roles.why: The root system fixes the Weyl group, the weight lattice and the double affine Hecke algebra.
The parameter $t = q^k$ turns the infinite product weight into the finite product, and $q \to 1$ gives the power $k$.

steps.slogan: Build the [double affine Hecke algebra](c:double-affine-hecke-algebra) and its polynomial representation on the weight lattice algebra.
steps.detail: Cherednik defines the algebra $\mathcal{H}$ of $R$ with parameters $q$ and $t = q^k$, generated by an affine Hecke algebra and the lattice algebra $\mathbb{C}[X]$. Its polynomial representation on $\mathbb{C}[X]$ uses Demazure-Lusztig operators.

steps.slogan: Diagonalize the commuting Cherednik operators to get nonsymmetric [Macdonald polynomials](c:macdonald-polynomial).
steps.detail: The operators $Y_b$ of $\mathcal{H}$ commute and act triangularly on $\mathbb{C}[X]$ for a suitable order on weights. Their joint eigenfunctions $E_\lambda$ are the nonsymmetric Macdonald polynomials, and symmetrization gives the polynomials $P_\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Show that the $E_\lambda$ are orthogonal for the constant term pairing with the Macdonald weight.
steps.detail: Let $\mu$ be the Macdonald weight, which is the finite product $\prod_{\alpha}(e^\alpha; q)_k$ at $t = q^k$, and $\langle f, g \rangle = \mathrm{CT}(f \bar g \mu)$. An anti-involution of $\mathcal{H}$ makes the $Y_b$ adjoint to conjugate operators, so eigenfunctions with different eigenvalues are orthogonal. The number $\langle 1, 1 \rangle$ is the [constant term](c:constant-term) of $\mu$.

steps.slogan: Compute the norms of the $E_\lambda$ from that of $1$ with intertwining operators.
steps.detail: Elements of $\mathcal{H}$ built from the affine Hecke generators send $E_\lambda$ to multiples of $E_{s_i \lambda}$ and $E_{\pi\lambda}$. Tracking the pairing through them gives $\langle E_\lambda, E_\lambda \rangle / \langle 1, 1 \rangle$ as an explicit product.

steps.slogan: Combine duality and evaluation formulas with the norm formula to fix $\langle 1, 1 \rangle$.
steps.detail: Cherednik's duality and evaluation formulas for $E_\lambda$ at the special point $q^{-\rho_k}$, together with the norm formula, determine $\langle 1, 1 \rangle$ in closed form. This is the product of Macdonald's constant term conjecture.

steps.slogan: Let $q \to 1$ to get the classical identity.
steps.detail: At $t = q^k$ the weight $\mu$ is a finite product whose limit as $q \to 1$ is $\prod_{\alpha}(1 - e^\alpha)^k$. The closed form of step 5 tends to $\prod_i \binom{k d_i}{k}$.

concepts.c:is-root-system: The root system fixes the product, the Weyl group and the double affine Hecke algebra.
concepts.c:weyl-group: Its degrees $d_i$ give the factors of the closed form.
concepts.c:constant-term: The identity computes the constant term of a product over the roots.
concepts.c:double-affine-hecke-algebra: Its polynomial representation carries the operators that diagonalize the pairing.
concepts.c:macdonald-polynomial: Their orthogonality and norms are what determine the constant term.

source.ref: I. Cherednik, Double affine Hecke algebras and Macdonald's conjectures, Annals of Mathematics 141 (1995), 191-216
source.note: The steps outline Cherednik's proof of the $q$-constant term conjecture; the limit $q \to 1$ gives the classical identity.

statement: Let a forager stay a time $t$ in each of many identical patches, with travel time $\tau > 0$ between patches and a differentiable [concave](c:concave-function) cumulative gain $g(t)$. Its long-term gain rate is $R(t) = g(t)/(\tau + t)$. A residence time $t^* > 0$ maximizes $R$ if and only if $g'(t^*) = R(t^*)$, and then the maximal rate is the [marginal rate](c:marginal-rate) $g'(t^*)$.

hypotheses.text: Every cycle of travel and residence is identical, so the long-term gain rate is $R(t) = g(t)/(\tau + t)$.
The cumulative gain $g\colon [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ is differentiable.
The gain function $g$ is [concave](c:concave-function): returns diminish with time in the patch.
The travel time $\tau$ between patches is positive.

conclusion: A residence time $t^* > 0$ maximizes $R$ exactly when $g'(t^*) = R(t^*)$, and then $\max R = g'(t^*)$.

proofs.name: First-order condition and tangent line
proofs.slogan: Differentiate the long-term rate to get the condition, and use the tangent line of the concave gain to show that the condition suffices.
proofs.scope: Residence times $t^* > 0$; the existence of a maximizer is not claimed, since a linear $g$ has none. The value $g(0) = 0$ of the usual model is not needed.

roles.why: Identical cycles make the total gain over $n$ cycles $n\,g(t)$ in time $n(\tau + t)$.
Differentiability of $g$ gives the derivative of $R$ at an interior maximizer.
Concavity puts the graph of $g$ under its tangent line.
A positive $\tau$ keeps $\tau + t$ positive, so $R$ is defined and we may divide by it.

steps.slogan: Write the long-term gain rate of residence time $t$ as $R(t) = g(t)/(\tau + t)$.
steps.detail: In $n$ identical cycles the forager gains $n\,g(t)$ in time $n(\tau + t)$. The ratio is $R(t)$ for every $n$, so it is the long-term rate.

steps.slogan: Set the derivative of $R$ to zero at a maximizer.
steps.detail: If $t^* > 0$ maximizes $R$, it is an interior extremum of the differentiable function $R$, so $R'(t^*) = 0$. Since $R'(t) = (g'(t)(\tau + t) - g(t))/(\tau + t)^2$, we get $g'(t^*) = g(t^*)/(\tau + t^*) = R(t^*)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the concave gain by its tangent line at $t^*$.
steps.detail: Let $t^* > 0$ satisfy $g'(t^*) = R(t^*) =: r$. Concavity gives $g(t) \le g(t^*) + g'(t^*)(t - t^*)$ for all $t \ge 0$. Since $g(t^*) = r(\tau + t^*)$, the right side equals $r(\tau + t)$.

steps.slogan: Divide by $\tau + t$ to show that $t^*$ maximizes $R$.
steps.detail: Step 3 gives $R(t) = g(t)/(\tau + t) \le r = R(t^*)$ for every $t \ge 0$. So $t^*$ is a maximizer, and the maximal rate is $r = g'(t^*)$.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives the condition at every maximizer, and step 4 shows that the condition forces a maximum. At a maximizer, $\max R = R(t^*) = g'(t^*)$.

concepts.c:concave-function: Concavity gives the tangent line bound that makes the condition sufficient.
concepts.c:marginal-rate: The marginal rate $g'(t^*)$ equals the best long-term average rate.

source.note: The elementary calculus proof of the model that E. L. Charnov introduced in Optimal foraging, the marginal value theorem, Theoretical Population Biology 9 (1976), 129-136.

statement: Let $\mu$ be a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) on $(X, \mathcal{B})$, let $T\colon X \to X$ be a [measure-preserving map](c:measure-preserving-map), and let $f$ be an [integrable function](c:integrable-function). Put $S_N f = \sum_{i<N} f \circ T^i$ and $E = \{x : \sup_{N \ge 1} S_N f(x) > 0\}$. Then $\int_E f \, d\mu \ge 0$.

hypotheses.text: $\mu$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) on the measurable space $(X, \mathcal{B})$.
The map $T\colon X \to X$ is [measure preserving](c:measure-preserving-map), and it need not be invertible.
The function $f$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function): $f \in L^1(\mu)$.

conclusion: The integral of $f$ over the set $E$ where some partial sum $S_N f$ is positive is nonnegative.

proofs.name: Garsia's proof
proofs.slogan: Truncate the supremum at level $n$, integrate a pointwise inequality using invariance of $\mu$, and let $n$ grow.
proofs.scope: The proof works on any $\sigma$-finite measure space and needs no ergodicity. It proves the claim for the sets $E_n$ first and then passes to $E$.

roles.why: The measure makes all integrals below defined, and sets $E_n \uparrow E$ pass to the limit.
Invariance of $\mu$ gives $\int M_n \circ T = \int M_n$.
Integrability makes $M_n$ integrable and supplies the dominating function $|f|$.

steps.slogan: Truncate the maximum at level $n$ and set $E_n = \{M_n > 0\}$.
steps.detail: Let $S_0 f = 0$ and $M_n = \max(0, S_1 f, \dots, S_n f)$. Then $0 \le M_n \le \sum_{i<n} |f| \circ T^i$, which is integrable, and the sets $E_n = \{M_n > 0\}$ increase to $E$.

steps.slogan: Prove the pointwise inequality $f \ge M_n - M_n \circ T$ on $E_n$.
steps.detail: For $1 \le k \le n$ we have $S_k f = f + S_{k-1} f \circ T \le f + M_n \circ T$. On $E_n$ the value $M_n$ is the maximum of $S_1 f, \dots, S_n f$, so $M_n \le f + M_n \circ T$ there.

steps.slogan: Integrate over $E_n$ and use invariance of $\mu$ to get $\int_{E_n} f \ge 0$.
steps.detail: Since $M_n = 0$ off $E_n$ and $M_n \circ T \ge 0$, we get $\int_{E_n} f \ge \int M_n - \int_{E_n} M_n \circ T \ge \int M_n - \int M_n \circ T$. Measure preservation gives $\int M_n \circ T = \int M_n$, so the right side is $0$.

steps.slogan: Let $n \to \infty$ with dominated convergence to get $\int_E f \ge 0$.
steps.detail: The functions $f \mathbf{1}_{E_n}$ tend pointwise to $f \mathbf{1}_E$ and are bounded by the integrable function $|f|$. Dominated convergence gives $\int_E f = \lim_n \int_{E_n} f \ge 0$.

concepts.c:probability-measure: The measure defines the integrals and the sets whose integrals are compared.
concepts.c:measure-preserving-map: Invariance of the measure under $T$ cancels $\int M_n$ against $\int M_n \circ T$.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability makes the truncated maxima integrable and gives the dominating function.

source.note: A. M. Garsia's short proof of Hopf's maximal ergodic theorem (Journal of Mathematics and Mechanics 14 (1965), 381-382).

statement: Let $F$ be a field of characteristic not $2$ and $n \ge 0$. The norm residue map $K^M_n(F)/2 \to H^n(F, \mathbb{Z}/2)$ sends the symbol $\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ to the cup product $(a_1) \cup \dots \cup (a_n)$ of Kummer classes. It is an isomorphism between [Milnor K-theory](c:milnor-k-theory) mod $2$ and [Galois cohomology](c:galois-cohomology).

hypotheses.text: $F$ is a field of characteristic different from $2$.
The degree $n$ is a nonnegative integer.

conclusion: The norm residue map $K^M_n(F)/2 \to H^n(F, \mathbb{Z}/2)$ is bijective.

proofs.name: Motivic cohomology and Rost motives
proofs.slogan: Compare Milnor K-theory with motivic cohomology, reduce to Hilbert 90 for symbols, and prove it with the Rost motive and motivic Steenrod operations.
proofs.scope: The outline is for fields of characteristic zero; the case of characteristic $p \ne 2$ is a separate step of the cited literature. The conjecture's consequences for [quadratic forms](c:quadratic-form) are not treated.

roles.why: Characteristic not $2$ makes $\mathbb{Z}/2$ coefficients and Kummer classes available; the motivic tools are used over such fields.
The proof is an induction on the degree $n$ that starts with Kummer theory.

steps.slogan: Settle degrees $0$ and $1$ with Kummer theory.
steps.detail: For $n = 0$ both sides are $\mathbb{Z}/2$. For $n = 1$ the map is $F^\times/F^{\times 2} \to H^1(F, \mathbb{Z}/2)$, which is bijective by the Kummer sequence and Hilbert's Theorem 90.

steps.slogan: Rewrite both sides as [motivic cohomology](c:motivic-cohomology) groups of the field $F$.
steps.detail: The theorem of Nesterenko-Suslin and Totaro identifies $K^M_n(F)/2$ with $H^{n,n}(F, \mathbb{Z}/2)$. The norm residue map becomes the comparison map $H^{n,n}(F, \mathbb{Z}/2) \to H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(F, \mathbb{Z}/2)$ from motivic to étale cohomology.

steps.slogan: Reduce degree $n$ to Hilbert 90 for symbols by induction on $n$.
steps.detail: Assume the comparison in degree $n - 1$ for all fields. Then degree $n$ reduces to the vanishing of certain motivic cohomology groups of the Čech simplicial scheme of the Pfister quadric $X_a$ of a symbol $a \in K^M_n(F)/2$.

steps.slogan: Split the motive of the Pfister quadric to isolate the Rost motive $M_a$.
steps.detail: For a nonzero symbol $a$, Rost showed that the motive of $X_a$ is a sum of Tate twists of one summand $M_a$, the Rost motive. The motivic cohomology of $M_a$ is the input for the vanishing.

steps.slogan: Compute the motivic cohomology of $M_a$ with motivic Steenrod operations.
steps.detail: Voevodsky constructs reduced power operations on motivic cohomology with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ coefficients, with Adem relations and a Cartan formula. With the Milnor operations built from them he proves the vanishing needed for Hilbert 90.

steps.slogan: Conclude the comparison in degree $n$ and run the induction.
steps.detail: The vanishing gives Hilbert 90 for $K^M_n$, hence the comparison in degree $n$. By induction the norm residue map is bijective for every $n$.

concepts.c:milnor-k-theory: Its mod $2$ quotient is the source of the norm residue map.
concepts.c:galois-cohomology: It is the target of the norm residue map, computed through étale cohomology.
concepts.c:motivic-cohomology: It links both sides and carries the Steenrod operations used in the proof.
concepts.c:quadratic-form: Pfister quadrics, which come from quadratic forms, are the splitting varieties of symbols.

source.ref: V. Voevodsky, Motivic cohomology with Z/2-coefficients, Publications Mathematiques de l'IHES 98 (2003), 59-104
source.note: The steps outline Voevodsky's proof, which uses his reduced power operations (same volume, pages 1-57) and Rost's work on Pfister quadrics.

statement: Let $p$ be a prime and $\mathcal{A}_*$ the dual of the mod $p$ [Steenrod algebra](c:steenrod-algebra). For $p = 2$, $\mathcal{A}_* = \mathbb{F}_2[\xi_1, \xi_2, \dots]$ with $|\xi_i| = 2^i - 1$. For $p$ odd, $\mathcal{A}_* = \mathbb{F}_p[\xi_1, \xi_2, \dots] \otimes \Lambda(\tau_0, \tau_1, \dots)$, an [exterior algebra](c:exterior-algebra) factor, with $|\xi_i| = 2p^i - 2$ and $|\tau_i| = 2p^i - 1$.

hypotheses.text: The number $p$ is a prime.

conclusion: The dual $\mathcal{A}_*$ is the stated polynomial algebra, tensored with an exterior algebra when $p$ is odd.

proofs.name: Coaction on classifying spaces
proofs.slogan: Define the generators by the coaction on the cohomology of $B\mathbb{Z}/p$, show that their monomials span, and count dimensions to see that they form a basis.
proofs.scope: The outline is written for $p = 2$; odd primes are the same with the $\tau_i$ and the exterior factor added. The coproduct formulas, such as $\Delta \xi_n = \sum_i \xi_{n-i}^{2^i} \otimes \xi_i$ for $p = 2$, come from coassociativity of the coaction and are not part of this statement.

roles.why: The prime fixes the coefficient field and the degrees of the generators, and for odd $p$ adds the exterior generators.

steps.slogan: Dualize the [Steenrod algebra](c:steenrod-algebra) into a commutative [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) $\mathcal{A}_*$.
steps.detail: The Cartan formula gives $\mathcal{A}$ a cocommutative coproduct, so the dual of the finite type algebra $\mathcal{A}$ is a commutative Hopf algebra $\mathcal{A}_*$. The action of $\mathcal{A}$ on cohomology becomes a coaction of $\mathcal{A}_*$.

steps.slogan: Define $\xi_i$ by the coaction on the generator $x$ of $H^1(B\mathbb{Z}/2; \mathbb{F}_2)$.
steps.detail: In [mod 2 cohomology](c:mod-p-cohomology) $H^*(B\mathbb{Z}/2; \mathbb{F}_2) = \mathbb{F}_2[x]$ the coaction has the form $\lambda(x) = \sum_{i \ge 0} x^{2^i} \otimes \xi_i$ with $\xi_0 = 1$. This defines $\xi_i \in \mathcal{A}_*$ of degree $2^i - 1$. Dually, $\langle \xi_i, \theta \rangle$ is the coefficient of $x^{2^i}$ in $\theta(x)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the monomials in the $\xi_i$ span $\mathcal{A}_*$.
steps.detail: The algebra $\mathcal{A}$ acts faithfully on $H^*((B\mathbb{Z}/2)^k)$ in degrees at most $k$. The coefficient of $x_1^{2^{i_1}} \cdots x_k^{2^{i_k}}$ in $\theta(x_1 \cdots x_k)$ is $\langle \xi_{i_1} \cdots \xi_{i_k}, \theta \rangle$. So an element $\theta$ that pairs to zero with all monomials is zero, and the monomials span the dual.

steps.slogan: Count the dimensions of $\mathcal{A}$ in each degree with admissible monomials.
steps.detail: The admissible monomials $Sq^{i_1} \cdots Sq^{i_k}$ with $i_j \ge 2 i_{j+1}$ form a basis of $\mathcal{A}$ by Serre and Cartan. In degree $d$ there are as many as partitions of $d$ into parts $2^j - 1$, which is the dimension of $\mathbb{F}_2[\xi_1, \xi_2, \dots]$ in degree $d$.

steps.slogan: Combine spanning and the dimension count to get a polynomial algebra.
steps.detail: In each degree the monomials span $\mathcal{A}_*$, and their number equals $\dim \mathcal{A}_d$. So the monomials are linearly independent, and $\mathcal{A}_*$ is the polynomial algebra on the $\xi_i$.

concepts.c:steenrod-algebra: It is the algebra whose dual the theorem computes.
concepts.c:exterior-algebra: At odd primes the dual also has an exterior factor on the generators $\tau_i$.
concepts.c:hopf-algebra: The dual is a Hopf algebra, and its coaction defines the generators.
concepts.c:mod-p-cohomology: The cohomology of $B\mathbb{Z}/2$ is the test space where the generators are read off.

source.ref: J. Milnor, The Steenrod algebra and its dual, Annals of Mathematics 67 (1958), 150-171
source.note: The steps outline Milnor's proof for p = 2 (generators from the coaction on the classifying space, basis from a dimension count); the odd prime case is in the same paper.

statement: Let $M$ be a closed [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold), $A$ a unital [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) and $P$ an [elliptic](c:elliptic-operator) pseudodifferential operator between bundles of finitely generated projective [Hilbert $A$-modules](c:c-star-module) on $M$. Then the analytic index $\operatorname{ind}_a P$ and the topological index $\operatorname{ind}_t \sigma(P)$ in $K_0(A)$ agree modulo torsion.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a closed [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold).
$A$ is a unital [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra), and the bundles on $M$ have fibers that are finitely generated projective [Hilbert $A$-modules](c:c-star-module).
$P$ is an $A$-linear [elliptic](c:elliptic-operator) pseudodifferential operator of order $0$ between these bundles.

conclusion: The classes $\operatorname{ind}_a P$ and $\operatorname{ind}_t \sigma(P)$ are equal in $K_0(A) \otimes \mathbb{Q}$.

proofs.name: Embedding and Bott periodicity
proofs.slogan: Define both indices in $K_0(A)$ and compare them by the Atiyah-Singer embedding argument with Hilbert module coefficients.
proofs.scope: The statement modulo torsion, as in the original paper. Kasparov's [KK-theory](c:kk-theory) later gave equality in $K_0(A)$ itself.

roles.why: Compactness makes $P$ Fredholm on Sobolev modules, and the embedding $M \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ defines the Gysin map.
The algebra $A$ is the coefficient ring: indices live in $K_0(A)$ and the Fredholm theory is over $A$.
Ellipticity makes $P$ Fredholm and gives a symbol class that carries the index.

steps.slogan: Define the index of a [Fredholm operator](c:fredholm-operator) on Hilbert $A$-modules in $K_0(A)$.
steps.detail: After stabilization the kernel and cokernel of an $A$-linear Fredholm operator are finitely generated projective $A$-modules. The index is $[\ker] - [\operatorname{coker}] \in K_0(A)$, and it is invariant under compact perturbations and homotopies.

steps.slogan: Show that the analytic index of an elliptic operator depends only on its symbol class.
steps.detail: An elliptic $A$-operator of order $0$ is Fredholm on the Sobolev completions, which are Hilbert $A$-modules. Homotopic symbols give operators that differ by a homotopy and a compact perturbation, so $\operatorname{ind}_a$ defines a map $K^0_A(T^*M) \to K_0(A)$.

steps.slogan: Define the topological index with an embedding $M \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ and Bott periodicity.
steps.detail: The embedding gives a Gysin map $K^0_A(T^*M) \to K^0_A(T^*\mathbb{R}^N)$. Bott periodicity identifies the target with $K_0(A)$, and the composite is $\operatorname{ind}_t$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two indices by the Atiyah-Singer method with $A$-module coefficients.
steps.detail: As in the Atiyah-Singer proof, one shows that $\operatorname{ind}_a$ is unchanged by the Gysin map of an embedding and agrees with $\operatorname{ind}_t$ on Euclidean space. The comparison holds after tensoring with $\mathbb{Q}$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the indices agree in $K_0(A) \otimes \mathbb{Q}$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 to 4 give $\operatorname{ind}_a P = \operatorname{ind}_t \sigma(P)$ in $K_0(A) \otimes \mathbb{Q}$, so the two classes differ by a torsion element of $K_0(A)$.

concepts.c:smooth-manifold: Compactness and smoothness give Sobolev spaces, Fredholm operators and an embedding in $\mathbb{R}^N$.
concepts.c:c-star-algebra: Its $K$-theory $K_0(A)$ is the group that holds both indices.
concepts.c:c-star-module: Fibers of the bundles are Hilbert modules over $A$, replacing vector spaces.
concepts.c:elliptic-operator: Ellipticity gives the Fredholm property and the symbol class.
concepts.c:fredholm-operator: Its index $[\ker] - [\operatorname{coker}]$ is the analytic index in $K_0(A)$.
concepts.c:kk-theory: KK-theory later gives the equality without passing to rational coefficients.

source.ref: A. S. Mishchenko and A. T. Fomenko, The index of elliptic operators over C*-algebras, Izvestiya Akademii Nauk SSSR, Seriya Matematicheskaya 43 (1979), 831-859; English translation in Mathematics of the USSR-Izvestiya 15 (1980), 87-112
source.note: The steps outline the paper: Fredholm theory over A, the analytic index, the topological index through a Gysin map, and the comparison of the two.

statement: Let $S$ be a finite set of at least two points in the plane. Every point that is constructible from $S$ by [ruler and compass](c:ruler-and-compass-construction) is constructible from $S$ by compass alone. A line is given by two of its points and is never drawn.

hypotheses.text: $S$ is a finite set of at least two points in the plane.

The point $X$ arises from $S$ by finitely many [ruler-and-compass](c:ruler-and-compass-construction) steps, each of which adds an intersection point of lines through two constructed points and circles about a constructed center through a constructed point.

conclusion: The point $X$ is constructible from $S$ by compass alone.

proofs.name: Inversion
proofs.slogan: Build inversion with the compass alone and use it to turn each line into a circle, so that every intersection becomes a circle-circle intersection.
proofs.scope: A free auxiliary point may be chosen off any finite set of lines and circles, as in classical constructions. A compass cannot draw a line, so a line is represented by two of its points.

roles.why: Two points give a first circle and a first inversion circle, so the construction can start.
The construction adds only intersections of lines and circles, so three kinds of intersection must be reproduced.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to two compass-only intersection constructions.
steps.detail: A [ruler-and-compass](c:ruler-and-compass-construction) step adds an intersection of two circles, of a line and a circle, or of two lines. Circle-circle intersections are already compass steps. So it suffices to find line-circle and line-line intersections by compass alone, with a line given by two points and a circle by its center and a point.

steps.slogan: Construct the [inverse](c:inversion) of a point in a given circle with the compass alone.
steps.detail: Let $\omega$ have center $O$ and radius $\rho$, and let $d = |OP| > \rho/2$. The circle about $P$ through $O$ meets $\omega$ at $A, B$, and the circles about $A, B$ through $O$ meet again at $P'$ with $|OP'| = \rho^2/d$ on ray $OP$. For smaller $d$, double $OP$ by walking round a regular hexagon $m$ times, invert, and double the image $m$ times.

steps.slogan: Construct the inverse of a line or circle as a circle with known center and one known point.
steps.detail: Take $O$ off the line or circle $\gamma$. The image $\gamma'$ is a circle through the inverses of the points of $\gamma$. Its center is the inverse in $\omega$ of $O^*$, where $O^*$ is the reflection of $O$ in a line $\gamma$ or the inverse of $O$ in a circle $\gamma$. For a line $AB$, $O^*$ is the second intersection of the circles about $A$ and $B$ through $O$.

steps.slogan: Intersect the two inverse circles and invert the intersection points back.
steps.detail: Let $\gamma_1, \gamma_2$ be the two given curves with $O$ off both. The circles $\gamma_1', \gamma_2'$ have known centers and points, so their intersection points are compass-constructible. Inverting them gives $\gamma_1 \cap \gamma_2$; the point $O$ matches infinity and is dropped.

steps.slogan: Conclude by induction on the steps of the ruler-and-compass construction.
steps.detail: Each new point is a circle-circle, line-circle or line-line intersection of earlier points. Steps 2 to 4 construct it by compass alone. So $X$ is constructible by compass alone.

concepts.c:ruler-and-compass-construction: The theorem compares this construction with the compass-only construction.
concepts.c:inversion: Inversion turns lines into circles, which a compass can handle.

source.note: The inversion proof of the Mascheroni constructions, as in Courant and Robbins, What is Mathematics? (Oxford University Press, 1941).

statement: Let $F$ be a field, $\ell$ a prime different from the characteristic of $F$, and $n \ge 0$. The norm residue map $K^M_n(F)/\ell \to H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(F, \mu_\ell^{\otimes n})$ from [Milnor K-theory](c:milnor-k-theory) to [Galois cohomology](c:galois-cohomology) is an isomorphism.

hypotheses.text: $F$ is a field and $\ell$ is a prime different from the characteristic of $F$.
The degree $n$ is a nonnegative integer.

conclusion: The norm residue map $K^M_n(F)/\ell \to H^n(F, \mu_\ell^{\otimes n})$ is bijective.

proofs.name: Norm varieties and motivic operations
proofs.slogan: Reduce to Hilbert 90 for symbols, build Rost's norm varieties that split them, and prove the vanishing with the Rost motive and motivic operations.
proofs.scope: The outline is for fields of characteristic zero, with induction on $n$. For $\ell = 2$ it is Milnor's conjecture, and the Beilinson-Lichtenbaum statement is the equivalent form for [motivic cohomology](c:motivic-cohomology).

roles.why: The prime $\ell$ gives coefficients and roots of unity, and the motivic machinery is used over such fields.
The proof is an induction on the degree $n$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the norm residue map as the comparison of motivic cohomology with étale cohomology.
steps.detail: The theorem of Nesterenko-Suslin and Totaro gives $K^M_n(F)/\ell \cong H^{n,n}(F, \mathbb{Z}/\ell)$, and the norm residue map becomes the comparison map to $H^n_{\mathrm{et}}$. Suslin and Voevodsky show that bijectivity for all fields and degrees is equivalent to the Beilinson-Lichtenbaum statement.

steps.slogan: Reduce degree $n$ to Hilbert 90 for symbols by induction on $n$.
steps.detail: Assume the theorem in degree $n - 1$ for all fields. Then degree $n$ reduces to the vanishing of certain motivic cohomology groups of the Čech simplicial scheme of a splitting variety of a symbol $a \in K^M_n(F)/\ell$.

steps.slogan: Construct Rost's norm variety $X_a$ that splits the symbol $a$.
steps.detail: For a nonzero symbol $a$ over a field with no extensions of degree prime to $\ell$, a norm variety is a smooth projective variety of dimension $\ell^{n-1} - 1$ over which $a$ splits and which satisfies Rost's degree condition. Rost's chain lemma and degree formula are the main tools.

steps.slogan: Use the Rost motive of $X_a$ and compute its motivic cohomology.
steps.detail: Rost and Voevodsky construct a direct summand $M_a$ of the motive of $X_a$, the Rost motive, built from Tate motives. Its motivic cohomology is the key input for the vanishing.

steps.slogan: Apply motivic Steenrod operations and Milnor operations to prove the vanishing.
steps.detail: Reduced power operations act on motivic cohomology with $\mathbb{Z}/\ell$ coefficients and satisfy Adem relations. Voevodsky uses them with the Milnor operations $Q_i$ to control the motivic cohomology of $M_a$ and to prove the vanishing of step 2.

steps.slogan: Conclude degree $n$ and run the induction on $n$.
steps.detail: The vanishing gives Hilbert 90 for $K^M_n$, so the comparison holds in degree $n$. Induction on $n$ gives bijectivity of the norm residue map in every degree.

concepts.c:milnor-k-theory: Its quotient mod $\ell$ is the source of the norm residue map.
concepts.c:galois-cohomology: It is the target of the norm residue map.
concepts.c:motivic-cohomology: It links Milnor K-theory with étale cohomology and carries the operations used.

source.ref: V. Voevodsky, On motivic cohomology with Z/l-coefficients, Annals of Mathematics 174 (2011), 401-438; C. Haesemeyer and C. A. Weibel, The Norm Residue Theorem in Motivic Cohomology, Annals of Mathematics Studies 200, Princeton University Press, 2019
source.note: The steps outline the Voevodsky-Rost proof: Rost's norm varieties and Rost motives together with Voevodsky's motivic operations.

statement: For every $n \ge 0$ and every set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$: $A$ lies in the class $\Sigma^0_{n+1}$ of the [arithmetical hierarchy](c:arithmetical-hierarchy) if and only if $A$ is [computably enumerable](c:recursively-enumerable-set) relative to the $n$-th [Turing jump](c:turing-jump) $\emptyset^{(n)}$. Hence $A \in \Delta^0_{n+1}$ if and only if $A \le_T \emptyset^{(n)}$.

hypotheses.text: The level $n$ is a natural number.
The set $A$ is a subset of $\mathbb{N}$.

conclusion: $A \in \Sigma^0_{n+1}$ if and only if $A$ is c.e. in $\emptyset^{(n)}$, and $A \in \Delta^0_{n+1}$ if and only if $A \le_T \emptyset^{(n)}$.

proofs.name: Induction on the level
proofs.slogan: Prove both implications by induction on $n$, turning quantifiers into searches with the use principle and the jump into a complete set.
proofs.scope: The classes are $\Sigma^0_0 = \Pi^0_0 = $ computable relations, $\Sigma^0_{k+1} = \{\exists y\, R : R \in \Pi^0_k\}$ and $\Pi^0_k = $ complements of $\Sigma^0_k$. The case $n = 0$ is Kleene's normal form, and the step from $n$ to $n+1$ is the induction.

roles.why: The proof is an induction on $n$ that starts at the normal form for $n = 0$.
Both implications treat $A$ as an arbitrary set of numbers, given by a formula or by an oracle program.

steps.slogan: Settle $n = 0$: the $\Sigma^0_1$ sets are the computably enumerable sets.
steps.detail: A set is [computably enumerable](c:recursively-enumerable-set) if and only if it equals $\{x : \exists s\, R(x,s)\}$ with $R$ computable, where $R(x,s)$ says that the program halts on $x$ within $s$ steps. This is the claim for $n = 0$, because $\emptyset^{(0)} = \emptyset$.

steps.slogan: Record the two facts about the [Turing jump](c:turing-jump) $X'$ that the induction needs.
steps.detail: The set $X'$ is c.e. in $X$, and every set c.e. in $X$ is many-one reducible to $X'$. So a set c.e. in $X$ has a complement that is computable in $X'$. These facts hold for every [oracle machine](c:oracle-machine) computation relative to $X$.

steps.slogan: Show that a $\Sigma^0_{n+2}$ set is c.e. in $\emptyset^{(n+1)}$, using the induction hypothesis.
steps.detail: Write $A = \{x : \exists y\, R(x,y)\}$ with $R \in \Pi^0_{n+1}$. The complement of $R$ is $\Sigma^0_{n+1}$, so it is c.e. in $\emptyset^{(n)}$ by the induction hypothesis, and $R$ is computable in $\emptyset^{(n+1)}$ by step 2. A search over $y$ with this oracle enumerates $A$.

steps.slogan: Show that a set c.e. in $\emptyset^{(n+1)}$ is $\Sigma^0_{n+2}$, using the use principle.
steps.detail: Let $A = W_e^X$ with $X = \emptyset^{(n+1)}$. By the use principle $x \in A$ if and only if some finite string $\sigma$ and stage $s$ have $\Phi_{e,s}^{\sigma}(x) \downarrow$ and $\sigma$ agrees with $X$. By step 2 and the induction hypothesis $X$ is $\Sigma^0_{n+1}$, so agreement is a finite conjunction of $\Sigma^0_{n+1}$ and $\Pi^0_{n+1}$ facts, which is $\Delta^0_{n+2}$. The quantifier $\exists \sigma, s$ in front gives $\Sigma^0_{n+2}$.

steps.slogan: Derive the $\Delta^0_{n+1}$ statement from the $\Sigma^0_{n+1}$ statement.
steps.detail: A set is $\Delta^0_{n+1}$ when it and its complement are $\Sigma^0_{n+1}$, so both are c.e. in $\emptyset^{(n)}$. A set is computable in $X$ exactly when it and its complement are c.e. in $X$. So $A \in \Delta^0_{n+1}$ if and only if $A \le_T \emptyset^{(n)}$.

concepts.c:arithmetical-hierarchy: The classes $\Sigma^0_n$ count alternations of quantifiers and are the object of the theorem.
concepts.c:recursively-enumerable-set: Computably enumerable sets are the base level and the relativized right-hand side.
concepts.c:turing-jump: The jump of the previous level is the oracle that turns a quantifier into a search.
concepts.c:oracle-machine: Relative computations by oracle machines give the right-hand side of the equivalence.

source.note: The standard proof, as in R. I. Soare, Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees (Springer, 1987), Chapter IV; the theorem is due to E. L. Post (Bulletin of the AMS 50 (1944), 284-316).
